To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“We have developed a method to pattern fluorinated and PEG monolayers of different widths onto silicon substrates and have used these substrates to study the ability of the marine green alga Ulvato attach to surfaces with varying stripe widths.”

(1) The pattern of stripes was successfully transferred to the silicon wafers, (2) The PEGylated stripes were able to repel proteins from a protein solution in water, (3) The fluorinated stripes were able to attract and adsorb proteins from the protein solution in water and, (4) The fluorinated background was able to attract and retain Ulva cells from a seawater solution.

the patterned monomeric surfaces were able to resist the attachment of Ulva, that the width of the stripes was not an important factor in determining the extent of fouling, and that the chemistry of the background was more important than the chemistry of the stripes in determining the extent and pattern of fouling.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of novel surfaces that are able to present different chemical functionalities in a well defined and controllable way.
the development of patterned surfaces that can be used to study marine biofouling at the microscale.
the fabrication of patterned monolayer surfaces for use in fundamental biofoultion studies and the development of coatings for the protection of marine structures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no clear evidence that the scale of the patterned domains is a critical parameter in the biofouling of the monolayer surfaces.

the smallest stripe width of 5 μm was able to be detected and that the PEG stripes of 5 μ and 20 μm widths were more effective at inhibiting the adhesion of Ulva than their fluorinated counterparts of similar widths.
the smallest feature size of a surface patterned in a hydrophobic/hydrophilic fashion that the marine organism can detect is 2 μm.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the patterned monomolecular films can be produced and are stable for several weeks, but the marine organisms do not respond to the pattern.
the width of the stripes was not a determining factor for settlement, and the pattern was not a deterrent for attachment.
the smallest stripes that could be distinguished by the algal spores were 50 μm wide.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the width of the stripes needs to be larger than the size of the settling organism for the organism to be able to detect the surface pattern.
the scale of the patterned surface features must be larger than 20 μm to avoid the attachment of the green alga.
the width of the stripes that are able to be distinguished by marine organisms is in the 50–100 μm range.
